questions.q: Why is power-sharing desirable in a democracy? Give both prudential and moral reasons.
answer: Power-sharing is the very spirit of democracy, and it is desirable for two kinds of reasons.

answer.text: These are based on careful calculation of gains and losses. Power-sharing helps reduce the possibility of conflict between social groups, and since social conflict often leads to violence and political instability, sharing power is a good way to ensure the stability of the political order. Imposing the will of the majority over others may look attractive for a while, but in the long run it undermines the unity of the nation.

These call power-sharing valuable in itself. Power-sharing is the very spirit of democracy. A democratic rule involves sharing power with those affected by its exercise and who have to live with its effects. People have a right to be consulted on how they are to be governed. A legitimate government is one where citizens, through participation, acquire a stake in the system.

questions.q: Compare how Belgium and Sri Lanka dealt with the question of power-sharing.
answer: Belgium and Sri Lanka are both democracies, but they dealt with cultural diversity in opposite ways.

answer.text: Belgium has a complex mix of Dutch, French and German speakers. Its leaders recognised these differences and amended the constitution to give equal representation to different language groups in the central government, gave more powers to state governments, and set up a special community government elected on the basis of language. This accommodation prevented conflict.

In Sri Lanka the Sinhala majority sought to dominate the government, made Sinhala the only official language, and favoured Buddhism. The Tamil minority felt alienated, and their demands for autonomy were repeatedly denied, leading to a long and destructive civil war.

answer: Thus Belgium's sharing brought unity, while Sri Lanka's majoritarianism brought conflict.
